questions.explanation: The volume flow rate is Q = A v, so v = Q/A = (0.0020 m^3/s)/(0.010 m^2) = 0.20 m/s. questions.explanation: Continuity gives A1 v1 = A2 v2, so v2 = (0.020 m^2)(3.0 m/s)/(0.0050 m^2) = 0.060/0.0050 = 12.0 m/s. The flow-rate route confirms it: Q = A1 v1 = 0.060 m^3/s, and Q/A2 = 0.060/0.0050 = 12.0 m/s. The area ratio is 0.0050/0.020 = 0.25, so the speed has to rise by a factor of 4, and the tempting wrong answer multiplies by 0.25 instead of dividing, giving 0.75 m/s, which would mean a constriction slowed the water down.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I

questions.explanation: Continuity makes the throat the fastest section, since a wide area of 0.020 m^2 at 2.0 m/s carries 0.040 m^3/s through the smaller throat, and Bernoulli ties that higher speed to a lower pressure, so P2 reads lowest. Both wide sections have the same diameter and the same height, so P1 and P3 read the same and the pressure recovers after the throat; the tempting wrong answer that the far section has lost the most energy would need a friction loss that the steady-flow statement rules out. Depth below the top of the pipe is irrelevant, because all three taps sit on the same horizontal centreline.

questions.explanation: A liquid surface behaves like a stretched membrane and surface tension pulls it to shrink, so among all shapes holding a given volume the sphere wins, with a surface area of about 4.8e-4 m^2 for a drop of volume 1.0e-6 m^3, the smallest available. Gravity flattens a large drop, so only small drops in near-free fall come close to a sphere. The tempting wrong answers that credit gravity or air pressure both miss the membrane: a falling drop is nearly weightless, and the wax only stops the drop from spreading by not letting it wet the surface.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_I

questions.explanation: The curved wall pulls the wetting water up at a contact angle, and the narrower the tube the more that wall pull outweighs gravity, so the rise h = 2 gamma cos(theta)/(rho g r) grows as 1/r: halving the radius doubles the height, and a tube of radius 0.10 mm can lift water several metres. Material and wetting set gamma cos(theta) and so the scale of the effect, but the bore sets the size of it, which is why a wide glass tube shows nothing measurable. The tempting wrong answer blames the volume a tube holds, but the reading is a height set by a force balance.

questions.stem: Water rises in a narrow glass capillary but not at all in a wide glass tube of the same material. Which statement explains the difference?
questions.subject: PHYSICS_I

questions.explanation: Capillary rise varies as 1/r, so h2 = h1 (r1/r2) = (0.040 m)(0.20 mm/0.050 mm) = (0.040)(4.0) = 0.16 m. The product form confirms it: h1 r1 = 0.040 x 0.20 = 0.0080 mm m, and 0.0080/0.050 = 0.16 m, because the surface tension and wetting terms are identical for two tubes of the same glass. Multiplying by the radius ratio instead of dividing gives 0.010 m, and the common wrong belief is that a narrower tube simply cannot hold as much water, which is a volume statement and not a height statement.
questions.hint: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to the tube radius.
